cards.text: In Proverbs, Wisdom calls out like a woman at the city gates, inviting anyone who'll listen (Proverbs 8:1-4). Now she has built her house and carved out her seven pillars. SEVEN pillars, friend, and my last home was a junk drawer propped up by takeout menus.
Then she prepares her meat, mixes her wine and sets her table. I know that energy, friend: that's me at 5 a.m. with every oven in the bakery warming up.

cards.question: Wisdom has built her house, prepared her meat, mixed her wine and set her table. What is all that getting ready for?
True or false: Once her table is set, Wisdom waits quietly inside until someone finds her house.

cards.text: Not even close: she sends out her maidservants and calls out from the heights of the city. Wisdom isn't sending one quiet text, friend, she's the group chat AND the billboard.

cards.question: Wisdom is calling out from the heights of the city. Who is her invitation for?

cards.text: She says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” and then, “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed.” Lacking judgment is my whole résumé, friend, and she STILL wants me at her table.

cards.question: Wisdom's invitation comes with one thing her guests need to leave behind. What is it?
Wisdom makes a promise to the simple: leave your folly behind, and you will ___.

cards.text: Then the passage shifts to some straight talk: whoever corrects a mocker brings shame on himself, and whoever rebukes a wicked man taints himself. It's arguing with the reply-all guy, friend, and NOBODY leaves that thread clean.

cards.question: Proverbs 9 warns against rebuking a mocker. What will the mocker do if you rebuke him?
True or false: When you rebuke a wise man, he holds it against you.

cards.text: And then: “Instruct a wise man, and he will be wiser still; teach a righteous man, and he will increase his learning.” Correction makes the wise man BETTER, like a recipe you keep fixing until every batch comes out perfect.

cards.question: Next comes one of the best-known lines in Proverbs. What does it call the beginning of wisdom?

cards.text: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.” Wisdom starts with God, friend, not with a three-hour podcast.

cards.question: Then comes a promise: through wisdom your days will be multiplied, and ___ will be added to your life.
If you are ___, it's to your own advantage, but if you ___, you alone will bear the consequences.

cards.text: Now meet the other woman in this passage: “The woman named Folly is loud; she is naive and knows nothing.” Loud AND knows nothing, friend, that was me my first week in the bakery, yelling instructions at an oven that wasn't even on.

cards.question: True or false: Like Wisdom, Folly builds a house with pillars and sets a table for her guests.

cards.text: Nope, she just sits at the door of her house, on a seat in the heights of the city, the same heights Wisdom called from. Wisdom carved seven pillars, friend, and Folly pulled up a CHAIR.

cards.question: From her seat, Folly calls out to the people passing by. What kind of people are they?

answers.text: Those leaving through the city gates

cards.question: When Folly calls out to the simple, she uses the ___ words Wisdom used.

cards.text: Word for word: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” Then she adds, “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!”

cards.question: Wisdom offered a feast she prepared herself. What is Folly's line about stolen water and secret bread really selling?
Folly's guests walk in expecting something sweet. What is really in her house?

cards.text: “But they do not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.” Two women, two houses, the same words at the door, friend, and only one of those doors leads to life.

findings.problem: The joke stacks three images (one quiet text, the group chat, the billboard) into one comparison instead of using one.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: "Not even close" opens the card by shooting down the True answer on card 4. For a baker who picked True, that reads as a put-down of their answer.

Verse 8 says a rebuked wise man "will love you." The walkthrough never tells this. The True/False card only establishes that he doesn't hold it against you, and card 13 moves straight on to verse 9. The positive half of the contrast is lost.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: Verse 9 says "instruct" and "teach," but Papa Dorin sums it up as "Correction makes the wise man BETTER." That relabels the verse and ties it to verse 8's rebuke in a way the text leaves open.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: No earlier card mentions the LORD or anything about where wisdom starts. The card before is about instructing the wise. A baker can only get this from prior knowledge or luck. A story card should set it up first.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The statement is marked False, but the text never says Folly didn't build her house or set a table. Verse 14 even says she has a house, and verse 18 says she has guests. The answer depends on the text's silence and treats it as a denial.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open. Who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: "Nope, she just sits at the door" claims that sitting is all Folly does, which goes beyond verse 14. "Nope" also answers the baker's pick on card 2 in a dismissive way.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: "The same words at the door" doesn't fit Wisdom. She calls from the heights of the city and through her maidservants (9:3). Only Folly is at her door (9:14).

rule.text: Noticing. What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: The right answer "same" depends on both 9:4 and 9:16, but the card cites only Proverbs 9:16. The output format only shows single verses and hyphen ranges, and 9:4-16 would be far too wide.
findings.question: How should a choice card cite a right answer that rests on two verses that aren't next to each other (for example "Proverbs 9:4, 16"), or should it cite only the later verse?
